newsitem.title: UK: Slovakia aims to lower interbank interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia aims to lower interbank interest rates.

text.p: Slovakia, with a burgeoning current account deficit, aims to lower money market interest rates in the second quarter of this year and sees no reason to devalue the crown currency, senior officials said on Sunday.

National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) board member Elena Kohutikova said that with money supply stable and growing at less than 13 percent in the first three months of the year, down from a 20 percent increase in the same period of 1995, more attention would be paid to interest rates.

"We are not very happy with the situation but we have to prepare for the long-term perspective for the Slovak currency," Kohutikova said during a presentation at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
Interbank market rates are around 20 percent, having eased from record levels of around 30 percent at the end of March.

The central bank tightened its policy several times last year, culminating in a series of steps in late 1996 after the government approved a 1997 fiscal deficit of 3.7 percent of GDP for 1997, after a 0.4 percent surplus in 1996.

NBS deputy governor Marian Jusko said interest rates remained volatile. "I suppose that the second quarter will bring a stabilisation but I do not expect that the rate will go under 10 percent," he said.
He said the current account deficit was financed by the capital account.
The current account deficit grew in 1996 to $1.94 billion, or 10.2 percent of gross domestic product, prompting some analyst concern about a possible devaluation.
But Kohutikova said this was not the solution. "Devaluation is not, according to our thinking and our analysis, the mechanism to solve the current account deficit," she said .
She said the current account deficit would be reduced to five percent of GDP this year.
She also said there was no serious problem with short-term speculative capital in the economy and that its volume was limited to $200-300 million.
